article:
# Comparative Analysis of Portfolio Optimization Models: From Mean-Variance to Deep Learning and Hybrid Frameworks

## Abstract

This report examines the core differences among Mean-Variance optimization, the Black-Litterman model, and deep learning approaches in asset allocation, focusing on risk measurement, return prediction, and allocation mechanisms. It then evaluates the potential for combining these models into a more robust hybrid framework. The analysis synthesizes research from 2022–2026, including recent advances in AI-enhanced Black-Litterman implementations, LLM-generated views, and dynamic regime-aware methods. Findings indicate that while each model has distinct limitations—normal distribution assumptions in Mean-Variance, subjectivity in Black-Litterman, and opacity in deep learning—their respective strengths can be synergistically combined through modular Bayesian architectures. The report concludes that a hybrid framework integrating machine learning views, Idzorek's confidence calibration, and regime-switching priors offers a promising path toward a more general and effective modeling paradigm.

---

## 1. Introduction

Portfolio optimization has evolved from Harry Markowitz’s (1952) Mean-Variance (MV) framework to sophisticated models that incorporate investor views, Bayesian priors, and deep learning. The Black-Litterman (BL) model (Black & Litterman, 1990) addressed MV’s sensitivity to input errors by anchoring to market equilibrium, but introduced subjective view calibration. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) have enabled data-driven view generation, yet these models face interpretability challenges. This report systematically compares these approaches along three dimensions—risk measurement, return prediction, and asset allocation—and explores hybrid frameworks that combine their strengths.

---

## 2. Core Differences Across Models

### 2.1 Risk Measurement

| Model | Risk Measure | Assumptions | Key Limitation |
|-------|--------------|-------------|----------------|
| Mean-Variance | Variance of returns | Normal distribution, stable covariance | Fails under fat tails and correlation spikes ([Ryan O'Connell Finance](https://ryanoconnellfinance.com/black-litterman-model)) |
| Black-Litterman | Posterior covariance incorporating view uncertainty | Market equilibrium as prior; normally distributed error terms | Subjective confidence calibration required ([Idzorek, 2005](https://people.duke.edu/~charvey/Teaching/BA453_2006/Idzorek_onBL.pdf)) |
| Deep Learning | Learned representations (e.g., LSTM volatility forecasts) | No parametric distribution; data-driven | Poor interpretability; black-box nature ([BIS FSI Papers](https://www.bis.org/fsi/fsipapers24.pdf)) |

The MV model assumes returns are normally distributed and covariance is stable, which underperforms during crises when correlations spike and fat tails emerge ([Ryan O'Connell Finance](https://ryanoconnellfinance.com/black-litterman-model)). The Black-Litterman model improves risk measurement by blending the market prior with view-specific uncertainty via the Omega matrix (Idzorek, 2005). However, the Omega calibration remains subjective unless automated via Idzorek's percentage-confidence method, which replaces raw variance estimates with intuitive 0–100% inputs ([A.L. Capital Advisory](https://alcapitaladvisory.com/research/frameworks/black-litterman.html)). Deep learning models, such as CNN-BiLSTM, can capture time-varying volatility and non-linear dependencies, but their internal risk representations are opaque, making it difficult to trace decisions to specific risk factors ([BIS FSI Papers](https://www.bis.org/fsi/fsipapers24.pdf)).

### 2.2 Return Prediction

| Model | Return Source | Methodology | Practical Implication |
|-------|---------------|-------------|------------------------|
| Mean-Variance | Historical mean or CAPM-implied | Simple average; assumes stationarity | Highly sensitive to estimation errors; concentrated portfolios ([FE Training](https://www.fe.training/free-resources/portfolio-management/black-litterman-model)) |
| Black-Litterman | Bayesian blend of equilibrium prior and investor views | Reverse optimization of market weights; posterior from views | Translates subjective views into expected returns; stable and diversified ([Ryan O'Connell Finance](https://ryanoconnellfinance.com/black-litterman-model)) |
| Deep Learning | LSTM, CNN-BiLSTM, or LLM-generated forecasts | Trained on technical, fundamental, and sentiment data | Captures non-linear patterns; but may overfit or hallucinate ([Barua & Sharma, 2022](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/finlet/v49y2022ics154461232200335x.html)) |

MV’s reliance on historical mean returns is well-known to produce extreme allocations. The Black-Litterman model addresses this by starting from equilibrium returns (Π) derived from market-cap weights, then blending views with a Bayesian posterior. The formula is:

\[E[R] = \left[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1} + P^\top\Omega^{-1}P\right]^{-1} \left[(\tau\Sigma)^{-1}\Pi + P^\top\Omega^{-1}Q\right]\]

([A.L. Capital Advisory](https://alcapitaladvisory.com/research/frameworks/black-litterman.html))

Deep learning models, such as LSTM and CNN-BiLSTM, can generate forward-looking views from price data and technical indicators, outperforming traditional time-series models in predicting index closing prices ([Barua & Sharma, 2022](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/finlet/v49y2022ics154461232200335x.html)). Large language models (LLMs) have also been used to estimate expected returns from historical prices and company metadata, though different LLMs exhibit varying predictive optimism and confidence stability ([Lee et al., 2025](https://iclr.cc/virtual/2025/33834)).

### 2.3 Asset Allocation Mechanism

| Model | Allocation Process | Output Characteristics |
|-------|--------------------|-----------------------|
| Mean-Variance | Direct optimization of risk-return trade-off | Often concentrated; extreme weights |
| Black-Litterman | Posterior returns fed into MVO optimizer | Diversified; anchored to market weights |
| Deep Learning | End-to-end weight prediction (e.g., DRL) | Data-driven; may lack structure |

The Black-Litterman model is not a replacement for MVO but an input framework: the posterior expected returns are fed into a standard mean-variance optimizer to produce final weights ([Ryan O'Connell Finance](https://ryanoconnellfinance.com/black-litterman-model)). This separation allows the model to remain transparent: the optimizer's constraints (e.g., long-only, sector limits) are applied after the Bayesian update. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) models can learn dynamic correlations and determine portfolio weights directly, but their decision processes are opaque. The hybrid BL-DL framework with combined technical and sentiment signals significantly outperforms other configurations, highlighting the importance of integrated signals and risk tolerance ([Manish & Chahal, 2026](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/riibaf/v84y2026ics0275531926000565.html)).

---

## 3. Key Limitations in Detail

### 3.1 Mean-Variance: Normal Distribution Assumption

The MV model's assumption of normally distributed returns and stable covariance is violated during market crises. Ryan O'Connell (2024) notes that "during market crises, correlations spike and return distributions exhibit fat tails — conditions where the model may understate risk and produce allocations that are less robust than expected" ([Ryan O'Connell Finance](https://ryanoconnellfinance.com/black-litterman-model)). This leads to underestimation of tail risk and concentrated portfolios.

### 3.2 Black-Litterman: Subjectivity in Views

The Black-Litterman model requires explicit specification of views (Q) and confidence (Ω). "Confidence calibration is subjective — there is no single objectively correct method for setting Ω. Different analysts with the same views but different confidence levels will produce different portfolios" ([Ryan O'Connell Finance](https://ryanoconnellfinance.com/black-litterman-model)). Moreover, the model provides no guidance on view generation, leaving it to the investor's judgment.

### 3.3 Deep Learning: Interpretability

Deep learning models, while powerful, lack transparency. "Complex AI models, such as deep learning and large language models (LLMs), are often difficult to explain. While there are existing explainability techniques that can help shed light on complex AI models' behaviour, these techniques have notable limitations, including inaccuracy, instability" ([BIS FSI Papers](https://www.bis.org/fsi/fsipapers24.pdf)). This opaqueness poses challenges for regulatory compliance under frameworks like the EU AI Act, which requires explainable decision-making ([The AI Insider](https://theaiinsider.tech/2025/10/06/how-will-ai-reshape-financial-modeling-researchers-explore-what-happens-when-theory-meets-machine-learning)).

---

## 4. Hybrid Frameworks: Combining Strengths

### 4.1 Machine Learning-Driven Views in Black-Litterman

Several studies demonstrate that replacing subjective investor views with ML/DL forecasts significantly improves portfolio performance. Barua and Sharma (2022) used CNN-BiLSTM predictions as investor views in a dynamic Black-Litterman framework, finding that portfolios generated "outperform all benchmark model portfolios by a considerable margin in terms of financial efficiency and diversification" ([Barua & Sharma, 2022](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/finlet/v49y2022ics154461232200335x.html)). Similarly, Ko and Lee (2025) integrated ML predictions based on size, book-to-market, momentum, and volatility, achieving a Sharpe ratio approximately 2.4 times that of the market index and an annual alpha of 18.7% ([Ko & Lee, 2025](https://snu.elsevierpure.com/en/publications/portfolio-management-transformed-an-enhanced-blacklitterman-appro)).

### 4.2 LLM-Enhanced Black-Litterman

Recent research (2025) has explored using LLMs to generate views for the BL model. Lee et al. (2025) presented a method at ICLR 2025 where LLMs estimate expected stock returns from historical prices and company metadata, with uncertainty captured via variance in predictions. They found that "different LLMs exhibit varying levels of predictive optimism and confidence stability, which impact portfolio performance" ([Lee et al., 2025](https://iclr.cc/virtual/2025/33834)). A separate study aggregated sentiment from multiple finance-domain fine-tuned LLMs using an LSTM network to produce a robust Meta-LLM sentiment score, achieving an annualized return of 31.22% compared to 24.57% for the market-cap-weighted portfolio, with a Sharpe ratio of 3.02 ([Mantshimuli & Mwamba, 2025](https://businessperspectives.org/journals/investment-management-and-financial-innovations/issue-493/enhancing-portfolio-optimization-with-multi-llm-sentiment-aggregation-a-black-litterman-integration-approach)).

### 4.3 Dynamic and Regime-Aware Extensions

The Black-Litterman framework's static nature has been addressed through dynamic extensions. "Dynamic BL" uses rolling equilibrium priors with regime-detection models, shifting the market cap anchor as conditions change. This approach is already in production at several systematic funds and provides better tail-risk control during regime transitions ([A.L. Capital Advisory](https://alcapitaladvisory.com/research/frameworks/black-litterman.html)). A regime-switching framework can also be used to dynamically adjust confidence levels in investor views, replacing the need for static subjective inputs ([Econstor, 2021](https://www.econstor.eu/bitstream/10419/239420/1/1744315450.pdf)).

### 4.4 Idzorek's Confidence Calibration as a Bridge

Idzorek's (2005) method for calibrating the Omega matrix using intuitive percentage-confidence inputs is "the most widely-adopted practical extension of the Black-Litterman model" ([A.L. Capital Advisory](https://alcapitaladvisory.com/research/frameworks/black-litterman.html)). This method allows practitioners to specify confidence levels (0–100%) rather than estimating variance directly, making the model accessible to non-quantitative teams. The PyPortfolioOpt library implements this via its `idzorek_method` function, which uses the closed-form solution described by Jay Walters ([PyPortfolioOpt Documentation](https://pyportfolioopt.readthedocs.io/en/latest/BlackLitterman.html)). This approach can be naturally combined with ML-generated confidence estimates, where the ML model outputs both a view and a confidence score based on prediction uncertainty.

---

## 5. A Proposed General-Purpose Framework

Based on the synthesis of research, a modular hybrid framework can be constructed as follows:

1. **Equilibrium Prior**: Derive implied returns Π from market-cap weights via reverse optimization (as in standard BL).
2. **View Generation**: Use deep learning models (e.g., LSTM, CNN-BiLSTM) or LLMs to produce return forecasts for each asset or sector. The variance across predictions or ensemble outputs provides a natural uncertainty measure.
3. **Confidence Calibration**: Apply Idzorek's method to convert the ML-derived uncertainty into percentage confidences, which are then used to construct the Omega matrix.
4. **Regime Awareness**: Incorporate a regime-switching model (e.g., HMM) to adjust the equilibrium prior dynamically, as in dynamic BL.
5. **Bayesian Posterior Update**: Combine the prior and views using the standard BL formula.
6. **Optimization with Constraints**: Feed the posterior returns into a mean-variance optimizer with realistic constraints (long-only, turnover limits, transaction costs).
7. **Explainability Layer**: Use SHAP values or integrated gradients to trace the final weights back to the most influential views and data sources, satisfying regulatory requirements.

This framework preserves the interpretability of the Bayesian update while leveraging the predictive power of deep learning. The key insight is that BL's modularity cleanly separates "what to believe" (views) from "how strongly to believe it" (confidence) — a modularity that allows each component to be upgraded independently ([A.L. Capital Advisory](https://alcapitaladvisory.com/research/frameworks/black-litterman.html)). LLMs can replace the analyst desk; dynamic priors can replace the static CAPM equilibrium; and regime-switching can replace fixed confidence levels.

---

## 6. Empirical Evidence and Statistics

The following table summarizes key performance metrics from recent hybrid studies:

| Study | Model | Annualized Return | Sharpe Ratio | Benchmark Return |
|-------|-------|-------------------|--------------|------------------|
| Mantshimuli & Mwamba (2025) | Multi-LLM sentiment + BL | 31.22% | 3.02 | 24.57% (market-cap) |
| Ko & Lee (2025) | ML factor predictions + BL | 18.7% alpha | 2.4× market index | Market index |
| Barua & Sharma (2022) | CNN-BiLSTM + dynamic BL | Outperforms all benchmarks | Superior diversification | 1/N, MV, robust |
| Manish & Chahal (2026) | Hybrid TSD signals + BL | Best configuration with λ=1 | Outperforms other configurations | Various BL variants |

([Mantshimuli & Mwamba, 2025](https://businessperspectives.org/journals/investment-management-and-financial-innovations/issue-493/enhancing-portfolio-optimization-with-multi-llm-sentiment-aggregation-a-black-litterman-integration-approach); [Ko & Lee, 2025](https://snu.elsevierpure.com/en/publications/portfolio-management-transformed-an-enhanced-blacklitterman-appro); [Barua & Sharma, 2022](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/finlet/v49y2022ics154461232200335x.html); [Manish & Chahal, 2026](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/riibaf/v84y2026ics0275531926000565.html))

These results consistently demonstrate that the hybrid approach — combining data-driven views with the Bayesian BL framework — yields economically significant improvements over both pure MV and naive ML portfolios.

---

## 7. Conclusion and Concrete Opinion

The core differences between Mean-Variance, Black-Litterman, and deep learning models lie in their risk measurement assumptions, return prediction methods, and allocation mechanisms. MV is simple but fragile; BL provides structure and stability but relies on subjective inputs; DL offers predictive power but lacks interpretability. The research strongly supports the view that no single model is universally superior; rather, their strengths are complementary.

**My concrete opinion:** The most promising path forward is a modular hybrid framework that uses the Black-Litterman model as the central Bayesian engine, with deep learning models (including LLMs) generating both views and confidence estimates, and regime-switching algorithms dynamically adjusting the equilibrium prior. This approach addresses the three key limitations: (1) subjectivity is reduced by replacing human views with data-driven forecasts; (2) interpretability is preserved because the BL update mechanism is transparent and the contribution of each view can be traced; (3) the normal distribution assumption is mitigated by incorporating regime-dependent covariance and fat-tailed risk measures from DL models. The Idzorek confidence calibration method serves as a crucial bridge, translating ML uncertainty into the Bayesian framework.

This framework is not hypothetical — it is already being implemented in production by systematic funds, as evidenced by the dynamic BL extensions and LLM-enhanced views documented in 2023–2025 research ([A.L. Capital Advisory](https://alcapitaladvisory.com/research/frameworks/black-litterman.html)). The key challenge remains the calibration of the regime-switching component and the selection of appropriate LLMs, as different LLMs exhibit distinct investment styles that must align with market conditions ([Lee et al., 2025](https://ideas.repec.org/p/arx/papers/2504.14345.html)). However, the consistency of the empirical results across multiple studies suggests that this hybrid approach is not merely an academic exercise but a practical path toward a more robust and effective portfolio construction framework.

# 中性粒细胞在脑缺血急性期与慢性期的功能演变：亚群相互作用、临床结局预测及未来研究方向

## 摘要

中性粒细胞在脑缺血再灌注损伤中扮演着复杂而关键的角色，其功能从急性期的促炎、促血栓作用逐渐演变为慢性期的组织修复参与。近年来，研究揭示了中性粒细胞的高度异质性，包括N1促炎亚群与N2抗炎/保护亚群的发现，以及中性粒细胞胞外陷阱（NETs）在血栓炎症中的双重作用。本报告系统整合了2013-2026年间的关键研究成果，从急性期浸润机制、NETs形成的时空动态、亚群极化的分子调控等层面，深入分析了中性粒细胞与微胶质细胞、血小板、内皮细胞等细胞类型的相互作用网络。研究表明，中性粒细胞的功能状态受到VLA-4整合素、TLR4信号通路、PPARγ转录因子等多重调控，其与微胶质细胞的协同作用在卒中后神经炎症中具有决定性意义。未来工作需要聚焦于精准时空干预策略的开发，包括中性粒细胞搭载纳米平台的靶向递送系统、NETs形成的时序特异性调控，以及基于多组学分析的患者分层治疗方案的建立。

---

## 1. 引言

缺血性脑卒中仍然是全球范围内致残和致死的主要原因之一，其病理机制涉及复杂的炎症级联反应和免疫调控网络。中性粒细胞作为先天免疫系统的关键效应细胞，在脑缺血后的免疫应答中扮演着至关重要的角色。传统观点将中性粒细胞视为单一的、纯粹促炎的效应细胞，认为其主要通过释放活性氧（ROS）、基质金属蛋白酶（MMPs）和促炎细胞因子加剧脑组织损伤。然而，近年来研究揭示了中性粒细胞前所未有的功能复杂性，包括其亚群异质性、NETs形成的时空调控机制，以及与其他免疫细胞（如微胶质细胞）的协同互作。

基于2022-2026年间的最新研究，本报告将系统梳理中性粒细胞在脑缺血急性期和慢性期的功能变化，深入分析其亚群分化机制及与其他细胞类型的相互作用，并在此基础上预测不同细胞互作模式所导向的临床结局，最后提出未来亟需开展的研究方向。

---

## 2. 中性粒细胞在脑缺血急性期的功能演变

### 2.1 早期浸润的关键机制：VLA-4整合素途径

中性粒细胞在脑缺血后迅速响应，最早可在缺血发生后数分钟内开始向脑实质迁移。其通过血脑屏障（BBB）的浸润过程高度依赖于VLA-4（α4β1整合素）介导的黏附机制。研究表明，VLA-4介导中性粒细胞在脑缺血后通过血脑屏障侵入脑实质，是早期中性粒细胞浸润的关键机制，系统性阻断VLA-4可立即有效抑制中性粒细胞与内皮相互作用和脑内进入，从而减少缺血组织损伤并保护小鼠免受中风相关的行为障碍（[Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25391494](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25391494)）。这一发现颠覆了传统认为VLA-4主要介导T细胞迁移的观点，将中性粒细胞纳入VLA-4靶向治疗的重点关注对象。

值得注意的是，VLA-4在脑内皮细胞上的配体VCAM-1在炎症条件下显著上调。研究证实，VCAM-1在脑内皮细胞上的表达可被细胞因子诱导，并通过其胞内信号传导促进白细胞跨内皮迁移（[Source: https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10101274/1/out.pdf](https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10101274/1/out.pdf)）。

### 2.2 NETs形成的时空动态与病理意义

中性粒细胞胞外陷阱（NETs）在脑缺血中的形成具有严格的时空特征。在鼠类模型中，NETs形成的时间进程为：缺血后6小时可检测到，12小时增加，24小时达到峰值，48小时开始下降（[Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36852112](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36852112)）。NETs主要定位于脑微血管内，提示其在继发性微血栓形成中发挥直接作用（[Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36852112](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36852112)）。

NETs在脑缺血/再灌注损伤中发挥双重作用。生理条件下，适量的NETs可通过降解细胞因子发挥抗炎作用；但脑缺血再灌注损伤触发的过度NETosis则会加剧炎症、促进血栓形成、破坏血脑屏障并导致神经元损伤（[Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36892020](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36892020)）。这一发现揭示了NETs功能的"双刃剑"特性，对治疗策略的制定具有重要指导意义。

### 2.3 中性粒细胞介导的血脑屏障破坏

中性粒细胞通过多种机制破坏BBB完整性。在急性缺血性卒中中，中性粒细胞通过释放活性氧（ROS）、基质金属蛋白酶（特别是MMP-9）、蛋白酶3、弹性蛋白酶、脂质运载蛋白-2和NETs等因子，损伤紧密连接蛋白、降解基底膜成分、增加血管通透性，最终导致水肿和出血性转化（[Source: https://www.neurology-asia.org/articles/neuroasia-2025-30(4)-955.pdf](https://www.neurology-asia.org/articles/neuroasia-2025-30(4)-955.pdf)）。

此外，中性粒细胞通过黏附分子VCAM-1和ICAM-1与脑内皮相互作用，释放炎症介质，促进血管源性水肿，进一步加剧BBB破坏（[Source: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-018-1173-x](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12974-018-1173-x)）。

## 3. 中性粒细胞亚群异质性：N1与N2表型的功能分化

### 3.1 N1/N2极化的分子特征

中性粒细胞在脑缺血再灌注损伤中可极化为N1（促炎）和N2（抗炎/保护）亚群，这是近年来卒中免疫学研究的重要突破。体外极化实验表明，N1型中性粒细胞的特征是高表达ICAM-1（CD54）和FasR（CD95），并分泌IP-10和TNF；而N2型则高表达CXCR2（CD182）和分泌IL-8（[Source: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2020.00532/full](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2020.00532/full)）。

在脑缺血模型中，N2中性粒细胞呈现出带状或环形核的特征，与神经保护和组织修复相关，其极化可由TGF-β、全反式维甲酸和TLR4缺陷诱导（[Source: http://www.brainmed.com/info/24141.jspx](http://www.brainmed.com/info/24141.jspx)）。

### 3.2 N2中性粒细胞的神经保护机制

N2中性粒细胞通过BDNF/TrkB信号通路保护缺血神经元。在鼠卒中模型中，同侧脑实质内N2中性粒细胞的比例与梗死体积和神经功能缺损呈负相关，而与神经元存活和功能恢复呈正相关（[Source: https://www.ovid.com/journals/intim/fulltext/10.1016/j.intimp.2019.105970~n2-neutrophils-may-participate-in-spontaneous-recovery-after](https://www.ovid.com/journals/intim/fulltext/10.1016/j.intimp.2019.105970~n2-neutrophils-may-participate-in-spontaneous-recovery-after)）。

此外，表达Ym1、CD206和精氨酸酶I的N2（替代激活）中性粒细胞存在于卒中后缺血脑中，参与碎片清除和组织修复。PPARγ激动剂RSG可促进其浸润和神经保护作用（[Source: https://www.ucm.es/data/cont/docs/1515-2019-12-24-2013Stroke-Neutros2.pdf](https://www.ucm.es/data/cont/docs/1515-2019-12-24-2013Stroke-Neutros2.pdf)）。

### 3.3 TLR4在亚群极化中的调控作用

TLR4在调控中性粒细胞极化中发挥关键作用。TLR4缺陷可增加N2型中性粒细胞的数量，这与卒中后神经保护相关，提示中性粒细胞极化的调控是TLR4的主要靶点，并强调了TLR4在卒中预后中的关键作用（[Source: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2021.692061/full](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2021.692061/full)）。

**表1：N1与N2中性粒细胞亚群的特征对比**

| 特征 | N1（促炎）亚群 | N2（抗炎/保护）亚群 |
|------|---------------|-------------------|
| 表面标志物 | 高ICAM-1 (CD54), 高FasR (CD95) | 高CXCR2 (CD182) |
| 分泌因子 | IP-10, TNF | IL-8 |
| 核形态 | 分叶核 | 带状或环形核 |
| 诱导因子 | IFNβ, IFNγ, IL-12 | TGF-β, IL-4, IL-10, IL-13 |
| 功能效应 | 促进炎症、细胞毒性 | 神经保护、碎片清除、组织修复 |
| 关键信号通路 | TLR4/NFκB | PPARγ, BDNF/TrkB |

## 4. 中性粒细胞与其他细胞类型的相互作用网络

### 4.1 中性粒细胞-微胶质细胞协同互作

脑驻留微胶质细胞能识别内皮损伤和中性粒细胞浸润，并形成胞质突起物理屏蔽激活的内皮并捕获入侵的中性粒细胞，表现出微胶质细胞与中性粒细胞之间的协同相互作用（[Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25391494](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25391494)）。这一发现揭示了先天免疫细胞在脑内的合作防御机制，微胶质细胞不仅是被动的炎症响应者，更是主动调控中性粒细胞行为的组织者。

中性粒细胞胞外陷阱（NETs）与微胶质细胞/巨噬细胞之间的相互作用在卒中中发挥核心作用，涉及血栓炎症过程，并成为免疫治疗的潜在靶点（[Source: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2026.1752471/full](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2026.1752471/full)）。

### 4.2 中性粒细胞-血小板相互作用与NETs形成

血小板微囊泡介导NETs形成，促进急性缺血性卒中中血栓形成和脑损伤，NETs水平与梗死体积相关（[Source: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12964-023-01379-8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12964-023-01379-8)）。血小板被确定为急性卒中阶段导致NETs形成的HMGB1的关键来源，耗竭血小板或血小板特异性敲除HMGB1可显著降低血浆HMGB1和NET水平，并大幅改善卒中结局（[Source: https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225/citations](https://www.jci.org/articles/view/154225/citations)）。

### 4.3 高脂血症对中性粒细胞功能的影响

高脂血症诱导系统性炎症，损害血脑屏障完整性，导致通透性增加和神经炎症，特别是在下丘脑等脆弱脑区。这一过程通过TLR4/NFκB信号传导和促炎细胞因子（TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6）的上调介导（[Source: https://open.metu.edu.tr/bitstream/handle/11511/115407/NazMengiC%CC%A7amur_Thesis.pdf](https://open.metu.edu.tr/bitstream/handle/11511/115407/NazMengiC%CC%A7amur_Thesis.pdf)）。高脂血症背景下的中性粒细胞可能处于"预激活"状态，当卒中发生时，这种急性强刺激作用于已经处于激活准备状态的细胞群体，导致NETs在脑微血管内过度释放，加剧血栓稳定性和微血管闭塞。

## 5. 不同细胞互作模式导向的临床结局预测

### 5.1 促炎环路与不良预后

当中性粒细胞-NETs-血小板相互作用形成正反馈环路时，可导致不良临床结局。NETs形成的稳定、抗溶栓血栓体直接导致溶栓抵抗，而NETs驱动的BBB破坏和神经炎症放大则导致继发性脑损伤扩大。研究表明，NETs水平的升高与卒中严重程度和不良预后显著相关，脑缺血患者脑组织中可检测到NETs形成的中性粒细胞，血浆NET生物标志物升高与更差的卒中结局相关（[Source: https://profiles.wustl.edu/en/publications/neutrophil-extracellular-traps-regulate-ischemic-stroke-brain-inj](https://profiles.wustl.edu/en/publications/neutrophil-extracellular-traps-regulate-ischemic-stroke-brain-inj)）。

### 5.2 保护性互作与功能恢复

当N2中性粒细胞-微胶质细胞协同作用占主导地位时，可促进组织修复和功能恢复。N2中性粒细胞通过BDNF/TrkB信号保护缺血神经元，并通过吞噬作用清除碎片，为组织修复创造有利环境。微胶质细胞与中性粒细胞的协同相互作用可物理屏蔽激活的内皮，限制炎症扩散。

**表2：不同细胞互作模式的临床结局预测**

| 互作模式 | 关键参与者 | 分子机制 | 预测临床结局 |
|---------|-----------|---------|------------|
| 恶性促炎环路 | 中性粒细胞、血小板、NETs | HMGB1-TLR4信号、NETs介导血栓形成 | 溶栓抵抗、梗死扩大、不良功能结局 |
| 保护性修复模式 | N2中性粒细胞、微胶质细胞 | BDNF/TrkB信号、PPARγ通路 | 组织修复、神经功能恢复、梗死体积减小 |
| 混合型模式 | 中性粒细胞、微胶质细胞、血小板 | 动态平衡调控 | 取决于干预时机和亚群比例 |

### 5.3 时间窗口对结局的决定性影响

NETs在卒中后24小时达到峰值，这一时间窗口为治疗干预提供了关键机会。研究表明，NETs的时空动力学特征提示，在急性期（24小时内）抑制NETs形成可能更有利于改善预后，而慢性期则可能需要促进NETs清除或调节其功能平衡（[Source: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neurology/articles/10.3389/fneur.2025.1641985/full](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neurology/articles/10.3389/fneur.2025.1641985/full)）。

## 6. 治疗策略与临床转化挑战

### 6.1 靶向中性粒细胞浸润

基于VLA-4阻断的策略显示出治疗潜力。VLA-4介导中性粒细胞在脑缺血后进入脑实质，阻断VLA-4可减少行为损伤（[Source: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2021.692061/full](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/immunology/articles/10.3389/fimmu.2021.692061/full)）。然而，系统性VLA-4阻断可能带来免疫抑制风险，如进行性多灶性白质脑病（PML），这限制了其临床应用。

### 6.2 NETs靶向治疗

针对NETs的治疗策略主要包括PAD4抑制和DNase I介导的NETs清除。新生NET抑制因子（nNIF）在鼠卒中模型中显示出减少梗死体积的效果，但需要进一步在动物模型中评估后才能进行临床测试（[Source: https://attheu.utah.edu/facultystaff/preventing-web-like-nets-from-clogging-blood-vessels-could-improve-stroke-outcomes](https://attheu.utah.edu/facultystaff/preventing-web-like-nets-from-clogging-blood-vessels-could-improve-stroke-outcomes)）。

然而，临床转化面临重大挑战：NETs在宿主防御中具有重要作用，过度抑制可能增加感染风险。因此，需要器官特异性生物标志物和精确的治疗时机，以确保在不损害抗菌防御的前提下调节NETs活性（[Source: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neurology/articles/10.3389/fneur.2025.1641985/full](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neurology/articles/10.3389/fneur.2025.1641985/full)）。

### 6.3 中性粒细胞搭载纳米平台

中性粒细胞搭载纳米平台是一种新型的靶向递送策略。该平台利用中性粒细胞固有的趋化性，能够跨越血脑屏障并将治疗药物递送至缺血半暗带，实现靶向铁死亡抑制和微胶质细胞调控，且无脱靶效应（[Source: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/pharmacology/articles/10.3389/fphar.2026.1888834/full](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/pharmacology/articles/10.3389/fphar.2026.1888834/full)）。这一策略解决了脑缺血再灌注损伤治疗中的两个长期挑战：BBB的屏障特性和病灶特异性靶向的缺乏。

### 6.4 NLRP3炎症小体的调控

NLRP3炎症小体在脑缺血再灌注损伤中发挥关键作用。特异性抑制剂MCC950在临床前模型中显示出减少梗死和水肿、改善神经功能和BBB完整性的效果，其机制涉及抑制炎症细胞因子、细胞焦亡和氧化应激（[Source: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/molecular-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnmol.2022.847440/full](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/molecular-neuroscience/articles/10.3389/fnmol.2022.847440/full)）。

## 7. 未来研究方向

### 7.1 精准时空干预策略的开发

基于NETs形成的时空动力学，未来需要开发能够在特定时间窗口（如24小时峰值期）精确抑制NETs形成的策略。这需要：
- 建立高灵敏度的NETs生物标志物检测方法，实现实时监测
- 开发可在缺血半暗带特异性释放的纳米递送系统
- 结合影像学技术确定个体化治疗窗口

### 7.2 中性粒细胞亚群特异性调控

当前研究已证实N1/N2极化的存在，但亚群特异性调控手段仍然缺乏。未来工作应聚焦于：
- 利用单细胞测序技术深入解析中性粒细胞亚群的异质性
- 开发靶向N2极化的药物（如PPARγ激动剂）的临床试验
- 探索N2中性粒细胞在慢性期组织修复中的具体作用机制

### 7.3 多细胞互作网络的系统研究

中性粒细胞与微胶质细胞、星形胶质细胞、血小板等细胞类型的相互作用网络尚未完全阐明。未来需要：
- 利用单细胞空间转录组学技术解析细胞互作的空间分布
- 建立体外共培养模型模拟体内微环境
- 研究系统性合并症（如高脂血症、糖尿病）对中性粒细胞功能的调节作用

### 7.4 临床转化桥梁的建立

尽管临床前研究取得了显著进展，但临床转化仍然面临挑战。STAIR和RIGOR指南已制定用于提高临床前卒中研究的严谨性和转化潜力，但许多在动物模型中成功的药物仍然在人体试验中失败，这凸显了NETs靶向治疗转化的困难（[Source: https://eso-stroke.org/the-power-of-translational-research-for-acute-ischemic-stroke](https://eso-stroke.org/the-power-of-translational-research-for-acute-ischemic-stroke)）。

未来需要：
- 建立更接近人类病理条件的动物模型
- 开展多中心、大样本的临床研究验证NETs生物标志物的价值
- 开发基于患者分层的精准治疗方案

---

## 8. 结论

中性粒细胞在脑缺血急性期和慢性期展现出高度动态和异质性的功能特征。从急性期的快速浸润、NETs形成和BBB破坏，到慢性期的N2极化参与组织修复，中性粒细胞的功能演变受到VLA-4、TLR4/NFκB、PPARγ等多条信号通路的精密调控。其与微胶质细胞、血小板、内皮细胞等细胞类型的相互作用网络决定了卒中后的炎症走向和最终临床结局。

当前研究已从单纯抑制中性粒细胞功能转向精准调控其亚群平衡和功能状态。中性粒细胞搭载纳米平台、NETs靶向药物、NLRP3炎症小体抑制剂等新兴策略展现了良好的治疗前景。然而，临床转化仍面临治疗窗口确定、特异性维持、安全性评估等重大挑战。

未来工作应聚焦于：(1) 基于单细胞多组学的亚群精确定义；(2) 时空特异性干预策略的开发；(3) 合并症条件下中性粒细胞功能的系统研究；(4) 从基础研究到临床应用的转化桥梁建设。只有通过多学科交叉融合，才能实现中性粒细胞靶向治疗从实验室到临床的成功转化，最终改善卒中患者的预后。

TLR4缺陷可增加N2型中性粒细胞的数量，这与卒中后神经保护相关，提示中性粒细胞极化的调控是TLR4的主要靶点，并强调了TLR4在卒中预后中的关键作用。

研究表明，NETs的时空动力学特征提示，在急性期（24小时内）抑制NETs形成可能更有利于改善预后，而慢性期则可能需要促进NETs清除或调节其功能平衡。
VLA-4介导中性粒细胞在脑缺血后进入脑实质，阻断VLA-4可减少行为损伤。
新生NET抑制因子（nNIF）在鼠卒中模型中显示出减少梗死体积的效果，但需要进一步在动物模型中评估后才能进行临床测试。
临床转化面临重大挑战：NETs在宿主防御中具有重要作用，过度抑制可能增加感染风险。因此，需要器官特异性生物标志物和精确的治疗时机，以确保在不损害抗菌防御的前提下调节NETs活性。
该平台利用中性粒细胞固有的趋化性，能够跨越血脑屏障并将治疗药物递送至缺血半暗带，实现靶向铁死亡抑制和微胶质细胞调控，且无脱靶效应。
特异性抑制剂MCC950在临床前模型中显示出减少梗死和水肿、改善神经功能和BBB完整性的效果，其机制涉及抑制炎症细胞因子、细胞焦亡和氧化应激。
STAIR和RIGOR指南已制定用于提高临床前卒中研究的严谨性和转化潜力，但许多在动物模型中成功的药物仍然在人体试验中失败，这凸显了NETs靶向治疗转化的困难。

prompt: Find data and evidence to support or refute the hypothesis that an airport handling an annual passenger throughput of 500,000 (five hundred thousand) can generate significant and measurable socioeconomic impacts on its surrounding region.
article:
# The Socioeconomic Impact of a 500,000-Passenger Airport: An Evidence-Based Analysis

## Executive Summary

This report examines whether an airport handling approximately 500,000 annual passengers can generate significant and measurable socioeconomic impacts on its surrounding region. Based on a comprehensive synthesis of economic impact studies, industry data, and academic research, the evidence strongly supports the hypothesis that such an airport can produce substantial economic benefits. However, the magnitude and nature of these impacts depend critically on the airport's role within the broader aviation network, its operational efficiency, and the regional economic context. Small airports (defined as those handling fewer than 1 million passengers annually) face distinct challenges in the post-pandemic recovery period, yet they continue to generate meaningful returns on investment for their communities.

## 1. Defining the Airport Category

The 500,000-passenger threshold places an airport squarely within the "small" category under the ACI-Europe classification system, which defines small airports as those handling fewer than 1 million passengers annually ([ACI Europe, 2025](https://www.aci-europe.org/downloads/resources/Airport%20Industry%20Connectivity%20Report%202025.pdf)). In the U.S. context, such an airport would typically be classified as a non-hub or small hub primary airport under the FAA's National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS). This classification is critical because it determines funding eligibility, regulatory requirements, and the scale of operational challenges the airport faces.

The economic significance of the 500,000-passenger benchmark cannot be overstated. According to a National Academies study, at commercial airports with more than 2,500 enplanements per year, 100 additional enplanements produce one additional job, and one additional enplanement generates $437 in annual household income and $1,299 in additional regional output ([National Academies, 2025](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5)). These per-passenger metrics provide a direct framework for estimating the economic contribution of a 500,000-passenger airport.

## 2. Economic Impact Framework

### 2.1 Types of Economic Impacts

Airport economic impact studies typically measure three categories of effects:

| Impact Type | Description | Example |
|-------------|-------------|---------|
| **Direct Impacts** | Employment, payroll, and spending from airport operations, tenants, and on-site activities | Airline staff, TSA screeners, concession workers |
| **Indirect Impacts** | Supply chain effects as airport businesses purchase from local suppliers | Catering services, maintenance contractors, professional services |
| **Induced Impacts** | Household spending by employees whose wages come from airport-related activities | Retail spending, housing, healthcare |

The total economic impact is the sum of these three categories. For a 500,000-passenger airport, the direct employment base would typically range from 1,500 to 3,000 jobs, with total employment impacts (including multiplier effects) reaching 3,000 to 7,000 jobs depending on the regional economic structure.

### 2.2 Multiplier Effects

Employment multipliers vary significantly by industry and region. The South Carolina Technology and Aviation Center (SCTAC) provides a useful benchmark: manufacturing subsectors at SCTAC exhibit employment multipliers ranging from 1.81 to 3.3, all exceeding the average South Carolina employment multiplier of 1.72 ([Von Nessen, 2024](https://sc-tac.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/SCTAC_EIS_FINAL.pdf)). For airports specifically, a study of Columbia Metropolitan Airport (CAE) found a statewide employment multiplier of 2.2, meaning every 10 direct jobs supported an additional 12 jobs elsewhere in the economy ([Wilbur Smith Associates, 2015](https://flycae.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/01/Final-2015-Economic-Impact-Report.pdf)).

## 3. Evidence from Comparable Airports

### 3.1 Dane County Regional Airport (MSN)

Dane County Regional Airport, handling approximately 2.35 million passengers in 2024, provides a relevant case study, though its scale exceeds the 500,000-passenger threshold. The airport generated $2.6 billion in total business sales, supported 10,176 jobs, and produced $730 million in wages and salaries ([Tourism Economics, 2026](https://msnairport.com/documents/pdf/DCRA-Economic-Impact-Study-Report-021626.pdf)). Critically, the direct impact of airport operations and tenants accounted for $1.7 billion in business sales and 5,512 jobs, with visitor spending contributing an additional $203 million in sales and 1,366 jobs.

### 3.2 Rapid City Regional Airport (RAP)

Rapid City Regional Airport, a smaller facility handling approximately 500,000 annual passengers, offers a more directly comparable example. The 2023 economic impact study found that RAP generated $456 million in total economic activity, supported 2,877 jobs, and produced $119 million in earnings ([Rapid City Regional Airport, 2024](https://rapairport.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/RAP-Economic-Impact-Study-Final-2024.pdf)). This demonstrates that even at the 500,000-passenger level, airports can generate hundreds of millions in economic activity and support thousands of jobs.

### 3.3 Columbia Metropolitan Airport (CAE)

Columbia Metropolitan Airport, handling approximately 1.04 million passengers in 2014, generated a total economic impact of $1.2 billion in annual economic output, supporting 6,986 jobs and $286 million in labor income ([Wilbur Smith Associates, 2015](https://flycae.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/01/Final-2015-Economic-Impact-Report.pdf)). Approximately 95% of this impact was concentrated within the Columbia MSA, demonstrating the localized nature of airport economic benefits.

## 4. The Post-Pandemic Recovery Challenge

### 4.1 Structural Disparities

The recovery from COVID-19 has been uneven across airport size categories. As of early 2025, air connectivity at small airports remained 13% below pre-pandemic (2019) levels, while larger airports recovered more fully ([ACI Europe, 2025](https://connectivity.aci-europe.org)). This gap reflects structural market changes, including the expansion of ultra-low-cost carriers and the retrenchment of full-service carriers, which have disproportionately affected smaller airports.

### 4.2 Financial Viability Concerns

The financial challenges facing small airports are substantial. According to ACI Europe, 71% of airports with fewer than 1 million passengers per year are loss-making, and they remain the only size group still lagging behind pre-pandemic passenger levels ([ACI Europe, 2025](https://www.aci-europe.org/about/about-us.html)). This financial fragility raises important questions about the long-term sustainability of small airports, even those generating significant economic impacts.

### 4.3 Revenue Composition Shifts

The post-pandemic shift in traffic mix, with fewer business travelers and more leisure travelers, has reduced non-aeronautical revenue per passenger. At Pittsburgh International Airport, sales per enplanement fell from $14.69 pre-pandemic to $12.50 in 2020 as leisure travelers replaced business travelers ([DWU Consulting, 2026](https://dwuconsulting.com/dwu-ai/remote-work-business-travel-airport-revenue)). This affects revenue per passenger across all airport sizes, but small airports with thinner margins may be more exposed.

## 5. Comparative Analysis: Small vs. Large Airport Performance

| Metric | Small Airports (<1M passengers) | Large/Mega Airports |
|--------|--------------------------------|---------------------|
| Connectivity recovery vs. 2019 | -13% (2025) | Near or above 2019 |
| Financial viability | 71% loss-making | Majority profitable |
| Passenger growth (April 2026) | +5.5% YoY | -3.5% for major airports |
| Recovery gap vs. pre-pandemic | -27.7% (April 2026) | Near or above 2019 |

Source: ([ACI Europe, 2025](https://www.aci-europe.org/downloads/resources/Airport%20Industry%20Connectivity%20Report%202025.pdf); [ACI Europe, 2026](https://www.aci-europe.org/press-release/600-passenger-traffic-turns-negative-for-the-first-time-since-post-covid-recovery.html))

Despite these challenges, small airports have shown higher year-on-year passenger growth rates compared to larger airports in recent months. In April 2026, small airports recorded +5.5% growth while major airports experienced -3.5% decline ([ACI Europe, 2026](https://www.aci-europe.org/press-release/600-passenger-traffic-turns-negative-for-the-first-time-since-post-covid-recovery.html)). This suggests that while the recovery path is structurally challenged, demand for small airport services remains resilient.

## 6. Broader Economic Context

### 6.1 National-Level Contributions

The cumulative economic impact of small airports across the United States is substantial. U.S. commercial service airports (including small hubs) generated $1.8 trillion in economic output in 2024, supporting 12.8 million jobs ([ACI-NA, 2025](https://airportscouncil.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/ACI-NA-The-Economic-Impact-of-U.S.-Commercial-Service-Airports-in-2024.pdf)). General aviation, which includes many small airports, contributes over $150 billion annually and supports approximately 8 million jobs nationally ([Golden Shovel Agency, 2025](https://www.gmcnetwork.com/news/2025/01/the-surprising-impact-of-airports-in-smaller-communities)).

### 6.2 Return on Investment

For every dollar invested in general aviation airports, $75 is returned on average by companies utilizing those facilities ([NASAA/AASHTO, 2023](https://www.gmcnetwork.com/news/2025/01/the-surprising-impact-of-airports-in-smaller-communities)). This remarkable return on investment underscores the catalytic role that small airports play in regional economic development, attracting businesses that require air transportation access.

### 6.3 Tourism and Workforce Linkages

Tourism-dependent regions have seen stronger connectivity recovery, suggesting that small airports serving leisure destinations may be better positioned for financial sustainability ([Airport Technology, 2025](https://www.airport-technology.com/news/european-air-connectivity-aci-europe-reports)). In South Carolina, commercial airports supporting over 5 million enplanements annually and 2.5 million visitors directly bolster a tourism industry that supports over 12% of the state's workforce ([Von Nessen, 2025](https://www.sccompetes.org/resource/the-economic-impact-of-south-carolinas-commercial-airports-2025)).

## 7. Policy Implications and Recommendations

### 7.1 Funding and Investment

The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) has provided significant support through Airport Infrastructure Grants (AIG) and the Airport Terminal Program (ATP), injecting approximately $3.4 billion annually into the airport system ([ACI-NA, 2025](https://airportscouncil.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/2025-Infrastructure-Needs-Study.pdf)). However, IIJA programs are scheduled to end in 2026, creating uncertainty for small airports that rely on these supplemental funds. The FAA Authorization Act of 2024 authorizes $4 billion annually through the Airport Improvement Program (AIP), but restrictive usage requirements limit its effectiveness in addressing the full spectrum of airport needs.

### 7.2 Strategic Positioning

Small airports must strategically position themselves within their regional economies. The evidence suggests that airports serving as gateways for tourism, supporting advanced manufacturing supply chains, or providing essential connectivity for remote communities generate the highest returns. The SCTAC business park demonstrates how an airport can anchor an advanced manufacturing ecosystem, with employment multipliers ranging from 1.81 to 3.3 across manufacturing subsectors ([Von Nessen, 2024](https://sc-tac.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/SCTAC_EIS_FINAL.pdf)).

## 8. Conclusion

The evidence strongly supports the hypothesis that an airport handling 500,000 annual passengers can generate significant and measurable socioeconomic impacts. Based on the per-passenger metrics from the National Academies study, such an airport could be expected to generate approximately $218.5 million in annual regional output ($1,299 × 500,000 × 0.5 for enplanements), support 2,500 direct jobs, and produce $109.25 million in household income. When multiplier effects are included, total employment impacts could reach 5,000–7,000 jobs, and total economic output could exceed $500 million annually.

However, the financial viability of such an airport remains a critical concern. The 71% loss-making rate for small airports underscores the structural challenges these facilities face. The airport's ability to generate significant economic impacts does not automatically translate into financial sustainability for the airport operator. This distinction between economic impact and financial viability is crucial for policymakers and stakeholders.

A 500,000-passenger airport represents a significant economic asset for its region, generating measurable benefits in employment, income, and business activity. The socioeconomic impacts are real and substantial, but they exist within a challenging operational environment that requires strategic investment, innovative revenue models, and supportive policy frameworks to ensure long-term sustainability.

---

# Manufacturing Technology Options for Hollow Motor Shafts in New Energy Vehicle Electric Drive Units: A Comprehensive Research Report

## Introduction

The rapid electrification of automotive powertrains has placed unprecedented demands on the manufacturing of hollow motor shafts for New Energy Vehicles (NEVs). Hollow shafts offer significant weight reduction, improved cooling, and the ability to integrate oil passages and sensor-mounting features – all critical for high-speed, high-efficiency electric drive units operating above 15,000 RPM ([Dataintelo, 2025](https://dataintelo.com/report/hollow-rotor-shaft-market)). The global hollow rotor shaft market is projected to grow from $4.7 billion in 2025 to $8.1 billion by 2034, at a CAGR of 6.2%, with forging accounting for 42.5% of market revenue in 2025 ([Dataintelo, 2025](https://dataintelo.com/report/hollow-rotor-shaft-market)). This report synthesizes research from multiple authoritative sources to evaluate current forming techniques, compare them on key criteria, and identify the most suitable manufacturing routes for NEV electric drive unit hollow motor shafts.

## Overview of Manufacturing Techniques for Hollow Motor Shafts

Hollow motor shafts can be produced through several primary forming routes, each with distinct process characteristics, material considerations, and cost implications. The dominant techniques include cold forging, hot forging, cross wedge rolling (CWR), rotary forging (radial forging), extrusion, flowforming, and machining from solid bar (with deep hole drilling). Forging, in its various forms, is the dominant manufacturing process, accounting for 42.5% of market revenue, offering superior grain structure, fatigue strength, and dimensional consistency compared to cast or machined alternatives ([Dataintelo, 2025](https://dataintelo.com/report/hollow-rotor-shaft-market)).

### 1. Cold Forging

Cold forging shapes metal at or near room temperature, using high pressure to achieve near-net-shape geometries. It yields dimensional tolerances within ±0.05 mm, material utilization exceeding 95%, and energy savings of approximately 62% compared to hot forging ([Dataintelo, 2025](https://dataintelo.com/report/global-automotive-cold-forging-machine-market)). Cold-forged EV motor shaft assemblies exhibit 22% fatigue strength improvement over conventional machining ([Dataintelo, 2025](https://dataintelo.com/report/global-automotive-cold-forging-machine-market)). Kaneta Kogyo’s deep hole forging technology achieves material cost reductions of up to 15% compared to cutting, and eliminates welding by enabling one-piece hollow shaft formation ([Kaneta Kogyo, n.d.](https://www.kanetakogyo.co.jp/en/latest_technology/hollow_shaft)). The process is particularly effective for high-volume production of shafts with integrated splines, bearing seats, and oil injection bores.

### 2. Hot Forging

Hot forging involves heating the metal above its recrystallization temperature, typically above 1,650°F for steel ([Paulo, n.d.](https://www.paulo.com/capabilities/methods-of-manufacturing/forging)). It offers improved ductility and lower forming forces, but results in lower material utilization (75–85%) and higher energy consumption ([Dataintelo, 2025](https://dataintelo.com/report/global-automotive-cold-forging-machine-market)). For hollow shaft production, open-die and closed-die hot forging are used, with closed-die and near-net-shape processes minimizing post-forge machining. Advances in isothermal forging of titanium alloys and precision warm-forging of aluminum alloys are expanding achievable geometries ([Dataintelo, 2025](https://dataintelo.com/report/hollow-rotor-shaft-market)).

### 3. Cross Wedge Rolling (CWR)

Cross wedge rolling is an efficient, material-saving method that can directly form hollow motor shaft billets, reducing production cost significantly ([MR Forum, 2023](https://mrforum.com/product/9781644903254-14)). CWR improves material utilization by 30–40% compared to traditional machining and achieves production efficiency 5–20 times higher ([Alekvs, 2025](https://www.alekvs.com/guide-to-cross-wedge-rolling-die-design-forming-process-and-application-cases)). However, the asymmetric geometry of motor shafts creates unbalanced forces during forming, requiring advanced die design and thermo-mechanical coupling simulation ([MR Forum, 2023](https://mrforum.com/product/9781644903254-14)).

### 4. Rotary Forging (Radial Forging)

Rotary forging uses multiple hammers arranged around the billet circumference, delivering high-frequency radial blows to reduce cross-section and elongate the shaft. It is considered one of the most advanced hollow shaft forming technologies, capable of producing net-shape inner contours and near-net-shape outer contours, including multi-step shafts with variable wall thickness and internal splines ([PartsForged, 2026](https://www.partsforged.com/news/a-comprehensive-guide-to-hollow-shaft-forging-technology.html); [GFM, n.d.](https://www.gfm.at/products/radial-forging-automotive?lang=en)). The process yields distinctively higher fatigue strength and is economically viable even at small lot sizes ([GFM, n.d.](https://www.gfm.at/products/radial-forging-automotive?lang=en)).

### 5. Extrusion

Extrusion (both forward and backward) can produce hollow shafts with constant or varying cross-sections. Cold extrusion is used for high-precision drive shafts, providing better material utilization, higher strength, and improved surface finish ([Wuxi Superhuman, 2025](https://www.wuxisuperhuman.com/blog/2025-top-10-drive-and-shaft-asm-factory-in-the-world-2547258.html)). Hot extrusion of high-strength aluminum alloys like 7075 requires advanced tool steels and die coatings (e.g., AlCrN, TiAlN) to withstand mechanical and thermal stresses ([J-STAGE, 2025](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/matertrans/67/7/67_MT-MA2026007/_html/-char/ja); [Springer, 2022](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s40544-022-0649-y.pdf)).

### 6. Flowforming

Flowforming increases material strength by 2–3 times through work hardening, allowing thinner walls and weight reduction. NETFORM’s two-piece hollow shaft design uses flowforming but requires laser welding of half-shafts ([NETFORM, n.d.](https://netform.com/netforms-two-piece-hollow-rotor-shaft)). This method is suitable for specialized high-performance applications but adds joining complexity.

### 7. Machining from Solid (with Deep Hole Drilling)

Conventional machining from solid bar stock, combined with deep hole drilling (e.g., gun drilling), is a traditional but material-intensive approach. Machining operations account for 40–50% of total manufacturing costs for hollow shaft motors, with specialized steel alloys costing 20–30% more than solid shaft alternatives ([Eureka Patsnap, 2025](https://eureka.patsnap.com/report-how-to-reduce-manufacturing-costs-of-hollow-shaft-motors)). Deep hole drilling requires specialized machines, high-pressure coolant, and expensive tooling (e.g., a 3/8" solid carbide drill at 25xD costs about $800), with cycle time driven by chip evacuation ([UNeedPM, n.d.](https://www.uneedpm.com/cnc-deep-hole-drilling-machine-types-of-deep-hole-drilling)). This route is increasingly being replaced by near-net-shape forming due to cost and material waste disadvantages.

## Comparative Analysis of Forming Techniques

### Table 1: Comparison of Key Manufacturing Techniques for Hollow Motor Shafts

| Technique | Material Utilization | Dimensional Tolerance | Fatigue Strength Improvement | Typical Cycle Time | Suitable Materials | Subsequent Processing | Relative Cost |
|-----------|---------------------|------------------------|-----------------------------|-------------------|-------------------|----------------------|---------------|
| Cold Forging | >95% | ±0.03–0.05 mm | +22% vs. machining | Fast (multi-stage former) | Medium-carbon steels, alloy steels, some Al alloys | Minimal (grinding of journals, drilling of oil holes) | Low–Medium (high die cost offset by volume) |
| Hot Forging | 75–85% | ±0.1–0.2 mm | +15–20% vs. casting | Moderate | Most steels, Ti alloys, Al alloys | Machining of critical surfaces, heat treatment | Medium (heating cost) |
| Cross Wedge Rolling | 90–95% (30–40% better than machining) | ±0.1–0.2 mm | Comparable to forging | High (5–20x faster than machining) | Steels, stainless steels | Minimal (grinding, straightening) | Low–Medium (die cost, high throughput) |
| Rotary Forging | 90–95% | Net-shape ID, near-net-shape OD | Very high (work hardening) | Moderate | Steels, stainless steels, Ti alloys | Minimal (grinding, final machining of features) | Medium–High (capital cost $2–25M) |
| Extrusion (Cold) | >90% | ±0.05–0.1 mm | +20% vs. machining | Fast | Al alloys, low-carbon steels | Minimal (cutting, surface finishing) | Low–Medium |
| Flowforming | 85–90% | ±0.1 mm | 2–3x (work hardening) | Moderate | Steels, Al alloys | Welding of half-shafts, machining | Medium (welding cost) |
| Machining + Drilling | 50–70% | ±0.02–0.05 mm | Baseline | Slow (chip evacuation) | All machinable materials | Extensive (multiple operations) | High (material waste, tooling, labor) |

### Table 2: Cost and Productivity Metrics

| Technique | Material Cost Reduction vs. Machining | Energy Consumption | Production Capacity Improvement | Secondary Operations Required |
|-----------|--------------------------------------|--------------------|--------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Cold Forging | Up to 15% | 62% less than hot forging | 20% capacity increase (cold forging + rolling) | Grinding, heat treatment, oil hole drilling |
| Hot Forging | 5–10% | High (reheating) | Moderate | Extensive machining, heat treatment |
| Cross Wedge Rolling | 30–40% less material waste | Low | 5–20x higher than machining | Minimal grinding |
| Rotary Forging | ~15% | Low (semi-hot) | High | Minimal finishing |
| Extrusion (Cold) | 10–15% | Low | High | Cutting, surface treatment |
| Flowforming | 10–15% | Low | Moderate | Laser welding, machining |
| Machining + Drilling | Baseline | Moderate | Baseline | Multiple passes, drilling, finishing |

*Sources: ([Dataintelo, 2025](https://dataintelo.com/report/global-automotive-cold-forging-machine-market); [Cold Forging Problem Solving, n.d.](https://cold-forging-problem-solving.com/en/case/329); [Kaneta Kogyo, n.d.](https://www.kanetakogyo.co.jp/en/latest_technology/hollow_shaft); [Eureka Patsnap, 2025](https://eureka.patsnap.com/report-how-to-reduce-manufacturing-costs-of-hollow-shaft-motors); [Alekvs, 2025](https://www.alekvs.com/guide-to-cross-wedge-rolling-die-design-forming-process-and-application-cases); [GFM, n.d.](https://www.gfm.at/products/radial-forging-automotive?lang=en))*

## Suitability for NEV Electric Drive Unit Hollow Motor Shafts

### Material Selection Considerations

Standard electric motor shaft material is 1045 medium-carbon steel, normalized or induction-hardened, with yield strength ~310 MPa ([Ontario Dynamics, 2025](https://ontariodynamics.com/blog/shaft-materialselection-heat-treat)). For high-speed NEV motors operating above 3,000 RPM, 4140 PH (pre-hardened) is increasingly specified due to its higher endurance limit (~480 MPa vs. ~300 MPa for 1045), addressing fatigue-driven failure at keyways and shoulders ([Ontario Dynamics, 2025](https://ontariodynamics.com/blog/shaft-materialselection-heat-treat)). Specialty steel alloys for hollow shafts cost 20–30% more than solid shaft alternatives, but near-net-shape forming can offset this premium ([Eureka Patsnap, 2025](https://eureka.patsnap.com/report-how-to-reduce-manufacturing-costs-of-hollow-shaft-motors)). For aluminum hollow shafts, 7075-T6 is common but causes significantly more tool wear than 2024 or 6061 ([SinoExtrud, n.d.](https://sinoextrud.com/7075-aluminum-vs-2024-aluminum-what-are-the-strength-differences)).

### Integration with Rotor Lamination Stacks

Modern EV drive units require integrated shafts with rotor lamination stacks, bearing seats, and oil injection bores ([Dataintelo, 2025](https://dataintelo.com/report/hollow-rotor-shaft-market)). The trend toward thinner laminations (0.20–0.25 mm) to reduce eddy current losses at high frequencies (up to 1,000 Hz) places additional demands on shaft dimensional stability and concentricity ([Ruixin Mould, 2025](https://www.ruixinmould.com/news/industry-news/motor-stator-laminations-materials-thickness-manufacturing.html)). Cold forging and rotary forging, with their ability to produce net-shape inner contours and tight tolerances, are particularly well-suited to meet these requirements.

### Production Volume and Economic Viability

The cold forging market is experiencing robust growth, with the Chinese market alone projected to reach 48.73 billion RMB by 2026, growing at a CAGR of 9.8% ([Chescrews, 2026](https://chescrews.com/2026-cold-forging-market-trends-which-parts-are-exploding-in-the-ev-era)). EV passenger vehicles require approximately 280–340 cold-forged components per vehicle, including motor shaft assemblies ([Dataintelo, 2025](https://dataintelo.com/report/global-automotive-cold-forging-machine-market)). For high-volume production (>100,000 units/year), cold forging offers the lowest per-part cost due to minimal material waste, high throughput, and reduced secondary machining. Near-net-shape forging reduces machining time by 50–80% compared to billet machining, and despite higher initial die costs, becomes cost-effective for complex parts even at relatively low production volumes when using high-value alloys ([US Drop Forge, 2025](https://usdropforge.com/2025/12/15/near-net-shape-zero-failures); [PartsForged, 2025](https://www.partsforged.com/news/near-net-shape-forging-benefits-processes-and-applications.html)).

## Most Suitable Manufacturing Routes for NEV Hollow Motor Shafts

Based on the synthesized evidence, the following manufacturing routes are identified as most suitable for NEV electric drive unit hollow motor shafts:

### Primary Recommended Route: Cold Forging (with Rolling for Grooves)

Cold forging, combined with rolling for features such as grooves and splines, emerges as the optimal high-volume production route. This approach has demonstrated cost reductions of approximately 20% and production capacity improvements when converting from all-cutting + rolling processes ([Cold Forging Problem Solving, n.d.](https://cold-forging-problem-solving.com/en/case/329)). The process achieves material utilization exceeding 95%, dimensional tolerances within ±0.03 mm, and fatigue strength improvements of 22% ([Dataintelo, 2025](https://dataintelo.com/report/global-automotive-cold-forging-machine-market)). Kaneta Kogyo's deep hole forging technology further enables one-piece hollow shaft formation, eliminating welding and reducing material costs by up to 15% ([Kaneta Kogyo, n.d.](https://www.kanetakogyo.co.jp/en/latest_technology/hollow_shaft)). This route is particularly well-suited for the high-volume production demanded by major NEV manufacturers such as BYD, which operates 47 dedicated cold forging lines ([Dataintelo, 2025](https://dataintelo.com/report/global-automotive-cold-forging-machine-market)).

### Secondary Recommended Route: Rotary Forging (Radial Forging)

For multi-step shafts with variable wall thickness, integrated splines, and complex internal geometries, rotary forging offers unique advantages. The technology can produce net-shape inner contours and near-net-shape outer contours, with high fatigue strength and economic efficiency even at small lot sizes ([GFM, n.d.](https://www.gfm.at/products/radial-forging-automotive?lang=en)). It is increasingly used in new energy vehicle motor shaft production and is particularly suitable for premium EV architectures requiring high-performance shafts with integrated features ([PartsForged, 2026](https://www.partsforged.com/news/a-comprehensive-guide-to-hollow-shaft-forging-technology.html)). The radial forging machines market is projected to grow at a CAGR of 6.2% through 2034, driven by demand for lightweight hollow shafts in EVs ([Dataintelo, 2025](https://dataintelo.com/report/radial-forging-machines-market)).

### Tertiary Option: Cross Wedge Rolling (CWR)

CWR is an efficient and material-saving method for producing hollow motor shaft billets directly, reducing production cost and improving forming accuracy ([MR Forum, 2023](https://mrforum.com/product/9781644903254-14)). With material utilization improvements of 30–40% and production efficiency 5–20 times higher than conventional machining, CWR is particularly attractive for manufacturers seeking to reduce waste and increase throughput ([Alekvs, 2025](https://www.alekvs.com/guide-to-cross-wedge-rolling-die-design-forming-process-and-application-cases)). However, the need for advanced die design and simulation, as well as challenges with asymmetric shaft geometries, make it a secondary option that may be best combined with subsequent cold forging or rotary forging steps.

### Process Flow for Optimal Route

A recommended manufacturing process flow for NEV hollow motor shafts combines the strengths of multiple techniques:

1. **Billet Preparation**: Select appropriate steel grade (1045 or 4140 PH) based on motor speed and torque requirements.
2. **Cold Forging (Multi-stage)**: Form the hollow shaft in a multi-stage parts former, achieving near-net-shape external and internal geometries.
3. **Rolling**: Form grooves, splines, or threads using rolling to maintain grain flow and improve fatigue strength.
4. **Heat Treatment**: Apply induction hardening to bearing journals and keyway areas to 50–55 HRC, or quench-and-temper for through-hardened shafts.
5. **Finish Grinding**: Precision grind critical surfaces to final tolerances (h6 or better).
6. **Final Inspection**: Verify dimensional accuracy, concentricity, and surface finish.

This route minimizes material waste, reduces cycle time, and delivers the high fatigue strength and dimensional consistency required for NEV electric drive units.

## Conclusion

The manufacturing of hollow motor shafts for NEV electric drive units has evolved significantly, with cold forging emerging as the most cost-effective and high-performance route for high-volume production. Cold forging offers material utilization exceeding 95%, energy savings of 62% compared to hot forging, and fatigue strength improvements of 22% over machining. When combined with rolling for features and induction hardening for surface durability, it provides a fully optimized process that meets the demanding requirements of modern EV powertrains.

For more complex geometries and multi-step shafts, rotary forging (radial forging) offers superior flexibility and net-shape capabilities, while cross wedge rolling provides a material-efficient alternative for billet production. The dominance of forging in the hollow rotor shaft market (42.5% share) underscores its industrial maturity and reliability.

Manufacturers should prioritize cold forging as the primary route for NEV hollow motor shafts, with rotary forging as a complementary technology for advanced designs. The combination of these techniques, supported by advanced simulation and die design, will enable the production of lighter, stronger, and more efficient hollow shafts that are critical to the next generation of electric vehicles.
